lead: Every pair of MOSFET terminals forms a small capacitor, and every time a gate switches, the driver must charge or discharge them through resistance. The gate oxide gives the largest capacitance; overlap and junction capacitances add to it, and how the gate capacitance splits between source, drain and body depends on the region. Series resistances of the source, drain, contacts and gate slow the charging further. Together these parasitics decide the dynamic behaviour: switching delay, dynamic power and how many gates one output can drive.
prereq: You need: the regions from MOS structure; nMOS and pMOS operating regions.

blocks.text: Gate and channel form a parallel-plate capacitor through the oxide: C<sub>ox</sub> = ε<sub>ox</sub>/t<sub>ox</sub> per unit area, and the gate area gives C<sub>ox</sub>·W·L. A handy unit is fF/µm²: with W and L in µm the product is in fF (1 F/m² = 1000 fF/µm²).
The source and drain diffusions spread a distance L<sub>ov</sub> under the gate edges, so the gate also overlaps them. Each overlap gives
Cov = Cox·W·Lov, stored in SPICE as CGSO and CGDO per unit width (Cov = CGSO·W)

Overlap capacitance is there in every region. Fringing field from the gate edge to the diffusions is usually folded into the same parameters. Because L<sub>ov</sub> does not shrink as fast as L, the overlap share of the gate capacitance grows as transistors get shorter.
The intrinsic part, C<sub>ox</sub>·W·L, connects the gate to whichever conductor sits under it. A simple model (often called the Meyer model) splits it as follows:

In cutoff there is no channel, so the gate sees the body through the oxide. In depletion the depletion capacitance is in series, so C<sub>gb</sub> is less than CoxWL; it approaches CoxWL only in accumulation. In the linear region the channel connects to both ends and the charge splits about equally. In saturation the channel is pinched off at the drain, so the drain loses its share and the source takes about two-thirds.

C<sub>gd</sub> matters more than its size suggests: in an inverter the drain swings opposite to the gate, so C<sub>gd</sub> is charged by both swings (the Miller effect) and counts about twice in delay estimates.

Source and drain form reverse-biased pn junctions with the body, giving C<sub>sb</sub> and C<sub>db</sub>. Each has a bottom part (per unit area) and a sidewall part (per unit perimeter), and both shrink as the reverse voltage V<sub>R</sub> grows:

C<sub>j0</sub> is the zero-bias capacitance, φ<sub>B</sub> the built-in potential (about 0.7 to 0.9 V) and m the grading coefficient (about 0.5 for the bottom, 0.33 for the sidewall). In SPICE these are CJ, CJSW, PB, MJ and MJSW; the drawn area and perimeter of each diffusion are given as AD, PD, AS and PS.

Resistance appears in series with the channel. Source and drain diffusions have a sheet resistance R<sub>sh</sub> (Ω per square), so a diffusion of length l and width W adds R<sub>sh</sub>·l/W. Each contact adds a contact resistance R<sub>c</sub>. The lightly doped drain extensions of short devices add more. The polysilicon gate is a distributed resistor along its width; a very wide gate behaves as an RC ladder, so layouts split wide transistors into several parallel fingers. Silicide on diffusions and gates cuts these resistances by about ten times.

examples.question: An nMOS has W = 1 µm, L = 0.25 µm, t<sub>ox</sub> = 4 nm and an overlap L<sub>ov</sub> = 0.02 µm at each side (ε<sub>ox</sub> = 3.45 × 10⁻¹¹ F/m). Find C<sub>ox</sub> in fF/µm², CoxWL, C<sub>ov</sub>, and C<sub>gs</sub>, C<sub>gd</sub> and the total gate capacitance in saturation; then C<sub>gs</sub> and C<sub>gd</sub> in cutoff.
steps: Saturation: C<sub>gs</sub> = ⅔ × 2.156 + 0.1725 = 1.4375 + 0.1725 = 1.610 fF; C<sub>gd</sub> = C<sub>ov</sub> = 0.1725 fF.
Total gate capacitance = C<sub>gs</sub> + C<sub>gd</sub> = 1.610 + 0.1725 = 1.78 fF (C<sub>gb</sub> = 0).
Cutoff: C<sub>gs</sub> = C<sub>gd</sub> = 0.17 fF; the rest of the gate couples to the body, up to 2.16 fF.
examples.answer: C<sub>ox</sub> = 8.63 fF/µm², CoxWL = 2.16 fF, C<sub>ov</sub> = 0.17 fF; in saturation C<sub>gs</sub> = 1.61 fF, C<sub>gd</sub> = 0.17 fF, total 1.78 fF; in cutoff C<sub>gs</sub> = C<sub>gd</sub> = 0.17 fF.

examples.question: The drain diffusion of the same transistor is 1 µm wide and 0.5 µm long, with CJ = 1.0 fF/µm², CJSW = 0.2 fF/µm (the edge under the gate not counted), φ<sub>B</sub> = 0.9 V, m = 0.5 bottom and 0.33 sidewall. Find C<sub>db</sub> at 0 V and at 1.8 V reverse bias. Then find the drain series resistance for R<sub>sh</sub> = 50 Ω/square and R<sub>c</sub> = 20 Ω.
steps: Area = 1 × 0.5 = 0.5 µm²; perimeter without the gate edge = 0.5 + 1 + 0.5 = 2 µm.
Resistance: the diffusion is 0.5 µm long and 1 µm wide, 0.5 square, so 50 × 0.5 = 25 Ω; plus R<sub>c</sub> = 20 Ω gives 45 Ω.
examples.answer: C<sub>db</sub> = 0.90 fF at 0 V and 0.57 fF at 1.8 V; drain series resistance ≈ 45 Ω.

traps: CoxWL is not the gate capacitance in every region: in saturation C<sub>gs</sub> ≈ ⅔CoxWL + C<sub>ov</sub> and C<sub>gd</sub> = C<sub>ov</sub>.
Leaving out overlap capacitance underestimates the load, most of all for short channels.
Junction capacitance falls with reverse voltage; quote the bias with the value.
Use one unit set: fF/µm² with µm, or F/m² with m.
A wide poly gate is a distributed RC line, not one resistor.

quiz.q: Name the five capacitances of a MOSFET.
quiz.a: C<sub>gs</sub>, C<sub>gd</sub> and C<sub>gb</sub> (gate oxide plus overlap), and the junction capacitances C<sub>sb</sub> and C<sub>db</sub>.

quiz.q: Why is C<sub>gd</sub> only the overlap capacitance in saturation?
quiz.a: The channel is pinched off at the drain end, so the channel charge is no longer connected to the drain; only the overlap of gate and drain remains.

quiz.q: Why does junction capacitance fall as the reverse bias rises?
quiz.a: Reverse bias widens the depletion layer, and a wider gap between the charge sheets gives less capacitance, as C<sub>j0</sub>/(1 + V<sub>R</sub>/φ<sub>B</sub>)<sup>m</sup>.

quiz.q: CoxWL = 4 fF and C<sub>ov</sub> = 0.2 fF. Find C<sub>gs</sub> and C<sub>gd</sub> in saturation and in the linear region.
quiz.a: Saturation: C<sub>gs</sub> = 2.67 + 0.2 = 2.87 fF, C<sub>gd</sub> = 0.2 fF. Linear: C<sub>gs</sub> = C<sub>gd</sub> = 2 + 0.2 = 2.2 fF.

quiz.q: A source diffusion is 0.8 µm long and 2 µm wide with R<sub>sh</sub> = 60 Ω/square and R<sub>c</sub> = 15 Ω. Find its series resistance.
quiz.a: 0.8/2 = 0.4 square, so 60 × 0.4 = 24 Ω; plus 15 Ω gives 39 Ω.

quiz.q: Why does the overlap share of the gate capacitance grow with scaling, and what does that do to delay?
quiz.a: CoxWL falls with L but L<sub>ov</sub> does not shrink as fast, so C<sub>ov</sub> becomes a larger fraction. C<sub>gd</sub> is overlap and is charged by both the input and the output swing, so it slows switching more than its size suggests.

beyond: Layout extraction tools compute these capacitances and resistances from the drawn shapes and pass them to circuit simulation. Modern models make the gate capacitance a smooth function of bias that conserves charge, and FinFETs add strong fringing from the gate to the raised source and drain. Search for "parasitic extraction" and "charge-conserving MOSFET capacitance model".

figure.caption: Where the parasitics of the worked transistor sit, with their values in saturation. The gate charge goes mostly to the source (1.61 fF); the drain sees only the overlap (0.17 fF), the junctions add C<sub>sb</sub> and C<sub>db</sub>, and the diffusions and contacts put resistance in series with the channel.
